name: Augustine's early psychology of sin
plain_explanation: Even as a young man, before becoming a Christian theologian, Augustine was preoccupied with the idea that he was deeply sinful -- famously agonizing for chapters over a boyhood prank of stealing pears he did not even want, treating it as proof of humanity's inherent wickedness.
precise_definition: The intense, self-scrutinizing sense of personal guilt recorded throughout Augustine's Confessions (e.g., Book II's extended treatment of the theft of pears as an act of 'gratuitous' wickedness, and Book I's claim that even infants are full of sin), which Russell connects to a broader psychological pattern rooted in Jewish theodicy (self-blame under national/personal suffering) and which becomes foundational to his mature theology of original sin and grace (Chapter IV).
why_it_mattered: Russell treats this personal, near-obsessive sense of sin as psychologically continuous with (and partly derivative of) the Jewish pattern discussed in Chapter I, and as the emotional wellspring of the theology of predestination and grace that would dominate Western Christianity, especially after the Reformation.
historical_origin: Documented by Augustine himself in the Confessions, written after his conversion, looking back on his pre-conversion life.
examples: Augustine's claim that infants at the breast are full of sin (gluttony, jealousy)
objections: Russell remarks that, to a modern mind, dwelling at such length on a boyhood prank 'seems morbid,' though he notes Gandhi's autobiography contains similar passages
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly informs Augustine's later doctrines of original sin, predestination, and grace developed in Chapter IV, later revived by Calvin and the Reformers.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Russell links the psychology of sin to the earlier Jewish substitution of divine punishment for national failure (Chapter I), now individualized rather than collective.
